nameStory: The Ring-billed Gull gets its name from the distinctive black band that circles its yellow bill like a wedding ring. This "ring" is one of the most reliable ways to identify this common gull, making it easy to remember once you've spotted it. The scientific name "delawarensis" honors the Delaware River, where early specimens were collected.
description: Ring-billed Gulls are medium-sized gulls that are among the most common and recognizable gulls in New England. These graceful birds have clean white heads and bodies with pale gray wings and backs. Adults typically measure about 17-21 inches long with a wingspan of around 4 feet. They're the classic "seagull" that most people picture, with their sleek build and confident demeanor around people.

idTips.label: Black ring on yellow bill
idTips.description: Look for the telltale black band that wraps completely around the bright yellow bill like a ring - this marking is crisp and unmistakable in good light

idTips.label: Yellow legs and feet
idTips.description: Bright yellow to orange-yellow legs that look almost plastic in their intensity, quite different from the pink legs of many other gulls

idTips.label: Pale gray wings with black wingtips
idTips.description: Wings appear silvery-gray with neat black markings at the tips, creating a clean contrast when the bird is in flight or standing with wings folded

idTips.label: Medium size and build
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more delicate than the bulky Herring Gulls, with a rounder head and less robust appearance overall

idTips.label: Dark eye with pale iris
idTips.description: Adults have dark eyes that appear almost black, giving them a gentler expression than the fierce yellow eyes of larger gull species

habitat: Ring-billed Gulls thrive around lakes, rivers, harbors, beaches, and coastal areas throughout New England. They're equally at home in urban environments, often seen in parking lots, parks, and anywhere food scraps might be found. These adaptable birds frequent both saltwater and freshwater environments, from Boston Harbor to mountain lakes in Vermont and New Hampshire.

seasonality.spring: Adults arrive with crisp breeding plumage showing the distinctive bill ring most clearly. They're often seen in flocks around harbors and lakes as ice melts.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification season with adults in full breeding plumage. Young birds may be present by late summer, showing mottled brown and gray feathers.
seasonality.fall: Large flocks gather along coastlines and major lakes. Mixed groups include adults and brown-mottled juveniles that can be confusing to identify.
seasonality.winter: Many remain year-round in New England, often concentrated around unfrozen harbors and urban areas. Adults may show slightly duller bill coloration but the ring remains visible.

funFact: Ring-billed Gulls have an incredible ability to drink both fresh and salt water thanks to special salt glands above their eyes that filter out excess salt - you can sometimes see them "crying" salt tears that drip from their nostrils after drinking seawater!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Herring Gulls, but Ring-billed Gulls are noticeably smaller with yellow (not pink) legs and that diagnostic black ring on the bill. Remember: "Ring around the bill, yellow legs pay the bill" - Herring Gulls have pink legs and no bill ring.
contextualKnowledge: These are the gulls that have learned to thrive alongside humans, often called "seagulls" even when found hundreds of miles inland around shopping centers and fast food restaurants. Their success in urban environments has made them one of the most familiar birds to casual observers.
compareHints: Ring-billed Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, lacking the Herring Gull's robust build and pink legs. They're much smaller than the massive Great Black-backed Gulls, and unlike the rare Iceland Gulls, Ring-billed Gulls have distinct black wingtips rather than very pale wing ends. The bill ring is unique among New England's common gulls.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's large gulls, American Herring Gulls are the 'Goldilocks' species - not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls, not as small as Ring-billed Gulls, but just right in the middle.

Among New England gulls, Great Black-backed Gulls dwarf the common Herring Gull in size and have much darker backs, while Ring-billed Gulls are significantly smaller with lighter grey backs and distinctive black rings around their bills.
Among New England's large gulls, Iceland Gulls are unique for their combination of medium size and extremely pale wing tips.
Among the large white-headed gulls, Lesser Black-backed Gulls are distinguished by their uniquely dark backs - darker than Herring Gulls but not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls.
Among New England's large gulls, Glaucous Gulls stand out for their pale wingtips—Herring Gulls and Great Black-backed Gulls both have bold black wingtips, while Ring-billed Gulls are much smaller.
Common Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, with yellow-green (not orange-red) bills and legs, plus a gentler facial expression.
Compared to the common Herring Gull, the Slaty-backed Gull has a noticeably darker slate-gray back and is generally larger and more robust.
Unlike Ring-billed Gulls which have a black ring on a yellow bill, Black-tailed Gulls have a red spot and often a black band near the bill tip.
Compared to the common Ring-billed Gull, Short-billed Gulls are smaller with cleaner wing tips and lack any dark markings on the bill.
Among the large white-headed gulls in its genus, the California Gull is most similar to the Ring-billed and Herring Gulls but sits between them in size.
Unlike the common white-bodied gulls of New England like Herring and Ring-billed Gulls, Heermann's Gull has the reverse color scheme with a dark body and white head.
